summary: Describes how Metro Ethernet Forum (MEF) Ethernet traffic parameters, as defined in MEF 10.1, can be expressed when using GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling. This lets a requested Ethernet connection state the traffic rates it needs.

plainLanguage.summary: When a network operator asks for a dedicated Ethernet path, the request has to say how much traffic that path must carry. This RFC defines the fields that carry that information inside the GMPLS reservation messages.

subtitle: How to state the traffic rates of an Ethernet service inside a GMPLS reservation request.

tldr.problem: GMPLS lets a signalling message carry parameters that belong to a specific technology, but there was no defined way to say how much Ethernet traffic a requested path must carry.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC and FLOWSPEC object for RSVP-TE, holding the switching granularity, the MTU and a bandwidth profile TLV with committed and excess rates and burst sizes.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from October 2010 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 3471 and RFC 3473 and registers new IANA code points for the object, its TLVs and its flags.

today: RFC 6003 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2010, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 3471 and RFC 3473 with the new Ethernet object, its TLV types and its two profile flags, all of which IANA registered in the GMPLS and RSVP-TE registries.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Per RFC 3471, Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching allows the inclusion of technology-specific parameters in signalling. This document introduces Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC and FLOWSPEC-specific objects in support of Metro Ethernet Forum Ethernet traffic parameters as specified in MEF 10.1, and ITU-T Ethernet Service Switching as discussed in RFC 6004.

For Ethernet Private Line services defined in MEF 6, these traffic parameters are applicable to each Ethernet Virtual Connection crossing a given port. For Ethernet Virtual Private Line services, also from MEF 6, they are applicable per Ethernet Virtual Connection with a single or multiple Class of Service, independent of its associated Virtual LAN ID or set of IDs. The association between an Ethernet Virtual Connection and the IDs is detailed in MEF 10.1, and the format and encoding of the ID, or set of IDs, is documented in the companion document RFC 6004.

This does not preclude broader use of the objects. They may also be used for signalling Ethernet Label Switched Paths in the Generalized Label Request, with the Switching Type field set to Layer 2 Switching Capability and the LSP Encoding Type field set to Ethernet.
sections.plainLanguage: GMPLS is a way to build paths across carriers' networks. When the path is an Ethernet circuit rather than an IP path, the request needs Ethernet-specific fields, and this RFC defines them.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
In GMPLS RSVP-TE, described in RFC 3473, the SENDER_TSPEC object is used on a Path message to indicate the bandwidth requested for the LSP being established, and the FLOWSPEC object is used on a Resv message to indicate the bandwidth actually reserved for it.

The Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC and FLOWSPEC object includes the Ethernet link type, meaning the switching granularity, of the requested LSP, and the MTU value for the LSP. Other information about the requested bandwidth characteristics of the LSP is carried in the Bandwidth Profile as a TLV within that object.

The Bandwidth Profile defines the set of traffic parameters applicable to a sequence of service frames, called the bandwidth profile parameters.

  • The Committed Rate indicates the rate at which traffic commits to be sent to the Ethernet LSP. It is described in terms of the CIR, the Committed Information Rate, and the CBS, the Committed Burst Size. CIR is the average rate, in bytes per unit of time, up to which the network is committed to transfer frames and meet its performance objectives. CBS sets a limit on the maximum number of information units, for example bytes, available for a burst of frames sent at the interface speed to remain CIR-conformant.
  • The Excess Rate indicates the extent by which the traffic sent on an Ethernet LSP exceeds the committed rate. It is described in terms of the EIR, the Excess Information Rate, and the EBS, the Excess Burst Size. EIR is the average rate, in bytes per unit of time and in excess of the CIR, up to which the network may transfer frames without any performance objectives. EBS sets a limit on the maximum number of information units available for a burst of frames sent at the interface speed to remain EIR-conformant.
  • The Color mode indicates whether the color-aware or color-blind property is employed by the bandwidth profile.
  • The Coupling flag allows the choice between two modes of operation of the rate enforcement algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: Two rates matter on an Ethernet circuit. The committed rate is the traffic the network promises to carry well. The excess rate is extra traffic it will carry if there is room, without promising anything about it. Each rate has a burst size, which caps how much can be sent in one short burst.

sections.title: The Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC Object
sections.content:
The Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC object has Class-Num 12 and Class-Type 6. Its layout is a 16-bit Length field, then the 8-bit Class-Num and 8-bit C-Type fields, then a 16-bit Switching Granularity field and a 16-bit MTU field, followed by one or more TLVs.

The Switching Granularity field indicates the type of link that comprises the requested Ethernet LSP. Value 0 means the granularity is provided in signalling, as described in RFC 6004. Value 1 is an Ethernet Port, for port-based service. Value 2 is an Ethernet Frame, for EVC-based service. Value 255 is reserved. Values 3 to 239 are to be assigned by IANA through a Standards Action, values 240 to 254 are reserved for vendor-specific use, and values 256 to 65535 are not assigned at this time.

The MTU field is a two-octet value indicating the MTU in octets. It must not take a value smaller than 46 bytes for Ethernet v2 or 38 bytes for IEEE 802.3.

The object must include at least one TLV and may include more than one. Each TLV has a 16-bit Type field, a 16-bit Length field, and a value. The Length field indicates the length in bytes of the whole TLV including the Type and Length fields, and a value whose length is not a multiple of four must be zero-padded so that the TLV is four-octet aligned. Type 0, Type 1 and Type 255 are reserved, Type 2 is the Ethernet Bandwidth Profile, and Type 3 is the Layer 2 Control Protocol. Values 4 to 239 are to be assigned by IANA, and values 240 to 254 are reserved for vendor-specific use.
sections.plainLanguage: The object has a fixed eight-octet header followed by a list of typed sub-objects. The header says what kind of path is being asked for, how big the frames may be, and the list carries the traffic numbers.

sections.title: The Ethernet Bandwidth Profile TLV
sections.content:
The Type 2 TLV specifies the Ethernet Bandwidth Profile and defines an upper bound on the volume of the expected service frames belonging to a particular Ethernet service instance. The Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC object may include more than one Ethernet Bandwidth Profile TLV.

Its value starts with a Profile byte, which is a bit vector of binary flags, followed by an Index byte and 16 reserved bits. Flag 1, bit 0, is the Coupling Flag and Flag 2, bit 1, is the Color Mode. Other flags are reserved and should be set to zero when sent and ignored when received. A flag set to 1 indicates that the corresponding metering profile is requested. When the Color Mode flag is 0 the bandwidth profile algorithm is said to be in color-blind mode, and when it is 1 the algorithm is in color-aware mode.

The Index field references bandwidth allocated for a given traffic class when a multiple-class LSP is being requested. Its value must correspond to at least one of the Class-Type values included either in the CLASSTYPE object of RFC 4124 or in the EXTENDED_CLASSTYPE object. A given index value can be associated with at most N Class-Type values of the EXTENDED_CLASSTYPE object, which is how one shared bandwidth profile can serve a set of Class-Types. Assigning an arbitrary value in the range 0x08 to 0xF8 associated with a set of Class-Type values allows a mapping to one of 248 predefined sets. A given index value can also be associated with a single Class-Type on a one-to-one basis, by assigning the three least significant bits of the Index field to the Class-Type value itself, which lies in the range 0x00 to 0x07. In that case a single Class-Type may map to a single dedicated bandwidth profile, in which case the object holds one Ethernet Bandwidth Profile TLV, or to multiple dedicated profiles, in which case it holds more than one TLV. A single LSP may combine shared and dedicated profiles. By default the Index field must be set to 0.

The remaining four fields are 32 bits each. The CIR is in units of bytes per second and must be greater than or equal to 0. The CBS is in units of bytes and, when the CIR is strictly greater than 0, must be greater than or equal to the maximum frame size. The EIR is in units of bytes per second and must be greater than or equal to 0. The EBS is in units of bytes and, when the EIR is strictly greater than 0, must be greater than or equal to the maximum frame size. All four are encoded as 32-bit IEEE single-precision floating-point numbers, as described in RFC 4506.
sections.plainLanguage: This sub-object holds the two rates and their burst sizes, plus two one-bit settings for how the network should police the traffic. The index byte says which class of traffic the numbers apply to, so that one request can carry different rates for different classes.

sections.title: Processing
sections.content:
The Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC and FLOWSPEC objects may be used for signalling an Ethernet LSP. For that, in the Generalized LABEL_REQUEST object of RFC 3471, the Switching Type field must be set to the value 51, which is L2SC, and the LSP Encoding Type field must be set to the value 2, which is Ethernet.

The Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC object carries the traffic specification generated by the RSVP session sender and should be forwarded and delivered unchanged to both intermediate and egress nodes. The Ethernet FLOWSPEC object carries reservation request information generated by receivers and, as with any FLOWSPEC object, flows upstream toward the ingress node.

Intermediate and egress nodes must verify that the node itself and the interfaces on which the LSP will be established can support the requested Switching Granularity, the MTU and the values included in the subobject TLVs. These nodes must be configured with the same predefined Class-Type sets as the index value signalled in the Index field of the Ethernet Bandwidth Profile TLV. If the requested values cannot be supported, the receiver node must generate a PathErr message with the error code Traffic Control Error and the error value Service unsupported.

In addition, if the MTU field is received with a value smaller than the minimum transfer unit size of the Ethernet frame, 46 bytes for Ethernet v2 and 38 bytes for IEEE 802.3, the node must generate a PathErr message with the error code Traffic Control Error and the error value Bad Tspec value.

Error processing of the CLASSTYPE object follows the rules defined in RFC 4124, and error processing of the EXTENDED_CLASSTYPE object follows the rules defined in the corresponding work in progress. A Label Switching Router that receives a Path message with the EXTENDED_CLASSTYPE object, recognizes the object and the particular Class-Type but detects a mismatch in the index values, must send a PathErr message towards the sender with the error code Extended Class-Type Error and the error value Class-Type mismatch.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router along the path checks that it can actually honour the request: that it supports the kind of Ethernet path asked for, that the frames fit, and that it has the class settings the index refers to. If it cannot, it answers the request with an error instead of accepting it.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
The document makes four kinds of allocation, all in the GMPLS and RSVP-TE registries.

First, two new Class Types for existing RSVP objects, taken from the Class Names, Class Numbers, and Class Types sub-registry of the Resource ReSerVation Protocol Parameters registry. Class Number 9, FLOWSPEC, gains Class Type 6, Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC. Class Number 12, SENDER_TSPEC, gains Class Type 6, Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC.

Second, a new sub-registry called Ethernet Switching Granularities holds the values that may appear in the Switching Granularity field. Values 0 to 2 are as described above, 3 to 239 are unassigned, 240 to 254 are reserved for vendor-specific use, 255 is reserved, and 256 to 65535 are not assigned at this time. The registration procedure is Standards Action.

Third, a new sub-registry called Ethernet Sender TSpec TLVs and Ethernet Flowspec TLVs holds the TLV type values carried in the Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC object. The same ranges apply, and the initial entries are Type 0 reserved, Type 1 reserved, Type 2 Ethernet Bandwidth Profile, Type 3 Layer 2 Control Protocol, and Type 255 reserved.

Fourth, a new sub-registry called Ethernet Bandwidth Profiles holds the bit flags carried in the Ethernet Bandwidth Profile TLV. Bits are numbered from bit 0 as the low order bit and are allocated by IETF Standards Action. The initial entries are bit 0, hex 0x01, Coupling Flag, and bit 1, hex 0x02, Color Mode.
sections.plainLanguage: The document asks IANA to register the new object, its sub-object types, the switching granularity values and the two flag bits, so that other vendors can extend them without collision.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document introduces no new security considerations beyond those of RFC 3473. GMPLS security is described in Section 11 of RFC 3471, which refers to RFC 3209 for RSVP-TE. Further detail on MPLS-TE and GMPLS security is in RFC 5920.
sections.plainLanguage: No new security rules. The existing RSVP-TE and GMPLS security guidance applies to these objects exactly as it does to the rest of the signalling.

fields.name: Class-Num
fields.desc: Object class number, 12 for SENDER_TSPEC and 9 for FLOWSPEC.

fields.name: C-Type
fields.desc: Class type, 6 for the Ethernet variant.

fields.name: Switching Granularity
fields.desc: The type of link that comprises the requested Ethernet LSP.

fields.name: MTU
fields.desc: MTU in octets. Must not be below 46 bytes for Ethernet v2 or 38 bytes for IEEE 802.3.

viz.caption: TLV types carried in the Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC object
The Ethernet Bandwidth Profile TLV, type 2

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: TLV type, 2 for the Ethernet Bandwidth Profile.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length in bytes of the whole TLV, including the Type and Length fields.

fields.name: Profile
fields.desc: Bit vector of flags: bit 0 is the Coupling Flag and bit 1 is the Color Mode.

fields.name: Index
fields.desc: References the bandwidth allocated for a given traffic class. Defaults to 0.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero when sent and ignored when received.

fields.name: CIR
fields.desc: Committed Information Rate in bytes per second, as a 32-bit IEEE single-precision float.

fields.name: CBS
fields.desc: Committed Burst Size in bytes. When CIR is above zero it must be at least the maximum frame size.

fields.name: EIR
fields.desc: Excess Information Rate in bytes per second, as a 32-bit IEEE single-precision float.

fields.name: EBS
fields.desc: Excess Burst Size in bytes. When EIR is above zero it must be at least the maximum frame size.

viz.caption: Flags in the Profile byte of the bandwidth profile TLV

items.label: Coupling Flag (CF)
items.desc: Bit 0. Allows the choice between two modes of operation of the rate enforcement algorithm.

items.label: Color Mode (CM)
items.desc: Bit 1. A value of 0 means color-blind mode and a value of 1 means color-aware mode.
